# How do social media feed algorithms affect attitudes and behavior in an election campaign?

## Abstract

We investigated the effects of Facebook’s and Instagram’s feed algorithms during the 2020 US election. We assigned a sample of consenting users to reverse-chronologically-ordered feeds instead of the default algorithms. Moving users out of algorithmic feeds substantially decreased the time they spent on the platforms and their activity. The chronological feed also affected exposure to content: The amount of political and untrustworthy content they saw increased on both platforms, the amount of content classified as uncivil or containing slur words they saw decreased on Facebook, and the amount of content from moderate friends and sources with ideologically mixed audiences they saw increased on Facebook. Despite these substantial changes in users’ on-platform experience, the chronological feed did not significantly alter levels of issue polarization, affective polarization, political knowledge, or other key attitudes during the 3-month study period.

Erratum 5 December 2024:

After publication of the Research Article “How do social media feed algorithms affect attitudes and behavior in an election campaign?” (28 July 2023, 10.1126/science.abp9364), the authors identified an issue with the variables that measure exposure to and engagement with untrustworthy sources on Instagram. Because of a processing error, data from accounts whose content participants may have seen during the study period, but that had been deleted by the time the participant dataset was created in 2022, were retroactively excluded from the metrics. Because participant platform data have now been permanently delinked from the user identifiers in this study, this error can no longer be fixed. The authors estimate that it should have a limited impact on the results reported in the paper, given that these deleted accounts only represent 6.8% of views received by all accounts identified as untrustworthy sources. The estimate of the proportion of participants’ Instagram feeds from untrustworthy sources in the control group (Fig. 2) is likely to be 0.014 rather than 0.013, as originally reported (Fig. 2 has not been revised). In addition, because this issue occurred independently from treatment assignment, the treatment effect estimates should not have been affected. This issue affects other results reported in the supplementary materials: Table S28, exposure to content from untrustworthy accounts as proportion of total views on Instagram, by connection type; Table S44, engagement metrics with content from untrustworthy accounts on Instagram, by connection type; Figures S16 and S17 and Tables S68 and S69, treatment effect on proportion of feed from untrustworthy sources on Instagram; and Figures S42 and S51, heterogeneous treatment effect results for proportion of feed from untrustworthy sources on Instagram. These tables and figures have not been revised. None of the results for Facebook were affected by this issue.
